Non-offense
non-uh-FENTS
noun / principle
Latin non (not) + offensa (a stumbling, a displeasure, a cause of injury), from offendere (to strike against, to stumble, to offend). The related Greek term is apros kopos (ἀπρόσκοπος) — without cause of stumbling, blameless, not giving offense; used in Philippians 1:10 (“sincere and blameless until the day of Christ”) and Acts 24:16 (Paul's own conscience before God and men). The companion term is skandalon (σκάνδαλον) — a stumbling-block, a snare — the setting of which Christ warns against in the severest terms (Matt 18:7).

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The biblical principle of non-offense is not the silencing of truth to avoid controversy, but the deliberate ordering of Christian liberty so as not to cause weaker brothers or unbelievers to stumble in their relationship with God. Paul's summary in 1 Corinthians 10:32 is the locus classicus: “Give no offense — either to Jews, or to Greeks, or to the church of God.” This is a tripartite pastoral directive covering every relationship the believer has: to the unconverted world and to the covenant community.

The principle is grounded in love, not in timidity. Romans 14–15 develops the argument at length: the strong in faith may eat anything and regard every day alike, but the exercise of that freedom must never become a stumbling-block for the weak. The strong must prefer their weaker brother's conscience over their own liberty (Rom 14:13) — not because the weak are always right, but because the goal of all Christian conduct is the edification of the community and the glory of God, not the vindication of one's freedom.

Christ's own warning in Matthew 18:7 grounds the seriousness of causing stumbling: “Woe to the world because of its stumbling blocks; for it is inevitable that stumbling blocks come — but woe to that man through whom the stumbling block comes!” The double “woe” signals that causing another person to stumble is not a minor pastoral misstep but a profound covenant violation. Philippians 1:10 frames the positive: the approved Christian life is characterized by discernment that distinguishes what is excellent and produces a life “sincere and blameless until the day of Christ” — the aproskopos life that gives no occasion for stumbling.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines offense as anything that causes anger, displeasure, or resentment; a stumbling-block; a violation of law or duty; the act of offending. Non-offense in the Christian sense is the positive ordering of conduct and liberty to avoid becoming an occasion of stumbling to others — a virtue rooted not in timidity but in covenant love for the neighbor.

OFFENSE, n. [L. offensa, from offendo, to stumble against.] 1. Displeasure; anger; the passion excited by an affront or injury. 2. A cause of displeasure or disgust. 3. A stumbling-block; a cause of sin or spiritual injury to another.

In the New Testament, the giving of offense (skandalon, a trap-trigger or stumbling-block) is among the most serious pastoral warnings: Christ pronounces woe upon those through whom stumbling-blocks come (Matt 18:7), and Paul makes the avoidance of offense one of the three great pastoral directives of 1 Corinthians (1 Cor 10:32, alongside giving glory to God and seeking others' profit).

NON-OFFENSE — the positive counterpart of offense: the life of the Christian that, by wise and loving ordering of liberty, gives no occasion for stumbling to the unconverted or to the weak in faith; the aproskopos life of Phil 1:10, without blame or cause of stumbling before God and men, characteristic of mature covenant love.

Key Scripture

1 Cor 10:32 — "Give no offense — either to Jews, or to Greeks, or to the church of God."

Matt 18:7 — "Woe to the world because of its stumbling blocks. For it is inevitable that stumbling blocks come — but woe to that man through whom the stumbling block comes!"

Rom 14:13 — "Therefore let us not judge one another anymore — but rather determine this: not to put an obstacle or a stumbling block in a brother’s way."

Phil 1:10 — "so that you may approve the things that are excellent — that you may be sincere and blameless until the day of Christ,"

Modern Corruption

Non-offense corrupts in two opposite directions: the capitulation error treats any pushback as a stumbling-block and surrenders true doctrine to keep the peace; the indifference error dismisses the pastoral principle entirely and uses Christian liberty as a license for selfishness.

expand to see more

The first corruption of non-offense is capitulation: treating any controversy, any hard doctrine, any clear biblical statement that provokes worldly displeasure as a “stumbling-block” to be removed. This error conflates the biblical stumbling-block — an obstacle to faith — with the scandal of the cross, which is not a stumbling-block to be removed but the very instrument of salvation. Paul is explicit: the cross is a stumbling-block to Jews and foolishness to Greeks (1 Cor 1:23), yet it is the power of God. The winsomeness enterprise in certain evangelical circles has produced a generation of communicators who smooth every edge of the gospel to avoid “giving offense” — but the offense they remove is often the cross itself. Non-offense is the servant of the gospel; when it suppresses the gospel, it has become a stumbling-block of its own kind.

The second corruption is indifference to the weak: the strong in faith using their liberty with no regard for its effect on those whose conscience cannot yet bear the weight of full freedom. The Corinthian strong who ate freely in idol temples, demonstrating their liberty in Christ, caused weaker believers to violate their own conscience (1 Cor 8:10–12) — and Paul calls this “sinning against Christ” (1 Cor 8:12). The liberty doctrine of the Reformation is real: the believer is free from the law as a means of justification. But that liberty is always exercised under the law of love (Gal 5:13–14), which orders freedom for the neighbor's good and the community's edification.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Rooted in the NT love-ethic that regulates the exercise of Christian liberty for the neighbor's good; the governing principle is not self-denial for its own sake but the deliberate subordination of personal freedom to the covenant obligation of love that is the fulfillment of all law.

expand to see more

Greek skandalon (σκάνδαλον) — a trap-trigger or stumbling-stick; the mechanism in a trap that trips the prey; extended to mean any obstacle that causes another to stumble or fall, whether into sin or away from faith; Christ's woe in Matt 18:7 targets those who set such traps for the vulnerable

Greek proskomma (πρόσκομμα) — a stumbling-block, a cause of offense; used in Rom 14:13 and 1 Pet 2:8; distinguished from skandalon but synonymous in pastoral use; the thing set in another's path that causes them to trip in their walk toward God

Greek apros kopos (ἀπρόσκοπος) — without stumbling-block; the adjective of the non-offense life; used in Phil 1:10 for the mature believer's approved character, and in Acts 24:16 for Paul's own conscientious conduct; the opposite of proskomma

Romans 14–15 — the sustained Pauline argument for liberty governed by love; the strong may eat meat offered to idols, but the strong must not exercise that liberty in the presence of the weak at the cost of the weak man's conscience; the goal is peace, mutual edification, and the glory of God (Rom 15:7)

1 Cor 10:23–33 — Paul's summary of the idol-meat principle, ending with the tripartite directive (v. 32) not to give offense to Jews, Greeks, or the church; grounded in v. 33: “not seeking my own profit, but the profit of the many, so that they may be saved” — missionary motivation governs apostolic conduct

Usage

"The Westminster Larger Catechism (Q&A 99) includes “taking heed that our liberty cause not the weak to stumble” under the duties required by the moral law — placing non-offense within the regulative framework of the commandments as a subset of love-of-neighbor, not as a mere social nicety."

"John Calvin's distinction in the Institutes (3.19.7–16) between offenses given and offenses taken is the classic Reformed analysis: an offense given is one the Christian causes by acting against the moral law; an offense taken is one the neighbor takes against lawful conduct. Non-offense addresses the first category; it does not require surrendering liberty to every sensitive conscience that takes offense at the legitimate exercise of freedom."

"The Puritan Richard Baxter in The Reformed Pastor makes pastoral non-offense a key virtue for ministers: the pastor must so order his public conduct that no unnecessary occasion of stumbling is given to the congregation or to the watching world — not timidity but love-shaped wisdom about the effect of the pastor's example on those under his care."
